wordsPreamble:
- English, spoken with Scouse, the fast, sing-song Liverpool accent shaped by Irish and Welsh migrants and the port. It sounds nothing like Manchester, 30 miles away, and locals would rather you didn’t compare them.
- Liverpool talks. Strangers chat at bus stops and bars, and teasing is friendly. A quick reply goes down better than a polite one.
- The city is red or blue: Liverpool FC or Everton. Families split down the middle, and someone will ask which you support.
- Many shops won’t sell *The Sun* newspaper, over its false 1989 coverage of the Hillsborough disaster, a stadium crush in which 97 Liverpool fans died. It is not a subject for jokes.

words.context: The all-purpose agreement: fine, good, that works. Said of a person, he’s sound is real praise.
Used with strangers as well as friends, and not considered sloppy. Cheers works just as well.
A greeting, not a question. “Sound, you?” closes it. Men add la (lad) and women often get queen or girl, all of it friendly.
The local goodbye, often stretched to ta-ra well. See you later works too.
The same reflex as the rest of England. Also means “what did you say?”, which you may need for the accent.
At a bar, stand where the staff can see you and wait your turn. Waving money or calling out gets you served later.

words.groupNote: Sorry works for apologising and for getting past. Excuse me is for asking something.

words.context: Some British people hear “Can I get” as too American. Liverpool barely notices; “Can I have” is the safe version.
That was boss covers food, a night out or a goal. Nothing to do with anyone’s employer.
Ask for the check and you’ll be understood, and marked as American.
Some restaurants add 10–12.5% to the bill. It should be printed on the bill and can be removed if you ask, so check before tipping on top.
Loo works, and bogs is cruder but common. Ask for the restroom and you’ll get a blank look.

words.groupNote: Standard on most doors. Pubs occasionally get creative with the signs.

words.context: Local buses take a tapped bank card or phone. Merseyrail, the local train network that loops under the city centre, needs a ticket from a machine or app before you board.
Also the hole in the wall. Bank-branded machines are free; some in shops and pubs charge a fee.
Contactless almost everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Still handy in older pubs, chippies and at the match, though card works nearly everywhere.
The cashier is asking if you want a bag, which costs extra. Say no thanks if you brought one.

words.meaning: Lad, used to address a man, friend or stranger: alright, la? Lid is the older version. Not rude in any way.
Delighted. I’m made up for you means you’re genuinely pleased for them. Nothing to do with lying or make-up.
Fake or counterfeit, as in a jarg watch or a jarg football shirt. Also a person who isn’t what they claim to be.
Food. Sailors used the word long before Liverpool did, and the port kept it. Is there any scran? means what’s to eat.
A protest at something unfair, said in a rising whine: ar eh, give us a go. Close to “oh, come on.”
